why: An FDE is handed a signed contract and a stated requirement that is almost always a solution somebody already picked - 'we need a dashboard', 'we need RAG over our SharePoint', 'we need an agent that does triage' - and building exactly that is the most common way an engagement ships on time and still fails. You are the only person on the vendor side who will sit with the analyst who does the work at 09:00 and the VP who signed the cheque at 16:00, so the single problem statement both of them will agree with does not exist until you go and manufacture it. Bad discovery does not fail loudly: you deliver in week six, adoption is zero by week ten, and the renewal conversation becomes about your product instead of their process.
prerequisites: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets from 'SRE fundamentals' (topic 20). A discovery success metric is an SLI with a baseline, a target and a measurement method, not an adjective.

The compliance vocabulary from 'Compliance: SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, PCI' (topic 64): BAA, DPA, sub-processor, data residency, right to erasure. You cannot ask constraint questions in a language you do not speak.
Enough Postgres and warehouse fluency (topics 29 and 36) to ask for a schema dump or a CSV export in the interview and have three defensible numbers out of it before the follow-up call.

A running demo you can put on screen in 90 seconds - Kaupex or DefenderMate - because FDE discovery is bidirectional: you probe, they react to something concrete, and you learn from the reaction, not from the compliment.
Five real humans who will give you 45 minutes each: ex-clients, friends running small businesses, an ops manager at a company you once contracted for. Booked before you start reading, not after.
Recording and transcription set up and tested end to end, plus a git repo for the write-ups. Discovering that your recorder was muted after interview three costs you the interview.

subtopics.name: Three different things called 'discovery' and which one you are doing
subtopics.learn: Separate sales discovery (does a deal exist, run pre-signature by an AE), product discovery (what should the product become, run continuously by PM/design), and delivery discovery - the FDE job - which starts after money changed hands and asks: what does this specific customer actually do all day, what will they let us deploy, and what has to be true in ninety days for them to renew. Know why the third is the hardest: the contract has already named a deliverable, your champion has already told their boss what it does, and your job is to find the real problem without making anyone look wrong for having mis-stated it. Write down, for your own engagement, the one sentence you would have to change in the SOW if discovery went badly - that is your risk surface.

resource.label: GOV.UK Service Manual - How the discovery phase works

subtopics.name: The Mom Test: three rules and the three signals you are being lied to
subtopics.learn: Internalise the three rules until you can apply them mid-sentence: talk about their life instead of your idea; ask about specifics in the past instead of generics or opinions about the future; talk less and listen more. Learn the three failure signals that mean the conversation produced nothing - compliments ('that's really cool', 'I love it'), fluff (generics, hypotheticals, 'I always/usually/never'), and ideas (their feature requests, which are data about a problem, never a spec). Practise the conversions out loud: 'would you use a tool that does X?' becomes 'walk me through the last time you did X'; 'how much would you pay?' becomes 'what do you spend on this today, and who signs that invoice?'; 'do you think this is a problem?' becomes 'what did you do about it last month?'

resource.label: The Mom Test (Rob Fitzpatrick) - book site

subtopics.name: Question taxonomy and a leading-question audit you can run on your own transcript
subtopics.learn: Classify every question you ask into open ('walk me through', 'what happened next', 'who else was involved'), closed (yes/no - fine for pinning facts, useless for exploring), leading (contains the answer: 'so that's slow, right?'), loaded (assumes a fact not in evidence: 'when the sync breaks, what do you do?'), and hypothetical (worthless: 'would you', 'could you see yourself', 'if we built'). Build a grep-able red-flag list - 'would you', 'do you think', 'wouldn't it be', 'how much would you pay', 'does that make sense', 'right?' - and after each interview run it over the transcript and count hits per hour. Set a target that trends downward across the five interviews and record the number in every write-up; an unmeasured habit does not change.

resource.label: NN/g - Open-Ended vs. Closed Questions in User Research

subtopics.name: Stakeholder map: buyer, champion, operator, gatekeeper, saboteur
subtopics.learn: Build a five-row map before interview one: economic buyer (owns budget, cares about the number in the board deck), champion (staked their reputation on you, will tell you what they want to hear), operator (does the work you are about to change, is the only source of ground truth about the workflow), gatekeeper (security, legal, procurement, platform - can veto and never gets invited), and the person who loses if this works (headcount, a tool they built, a fiefdom). Assign a different question set to each: the buyer gets 'what does this have to move for you to fund phase two', the operator gets 'show me the last five cases you handled', the gatekeeper gets 'what has to be true before you would sign off on a deployment in your VPC'. Explicitly answer 'who has not been in a room with us yet, and why' - the missing name is usually the one who kills the project in month three.

resource.label: Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework - Strategy (motivations, outcomes, stakeholders)

subtopics.name: Booking, consent, recording and the 45-minute session shape
subtopics.learn: Get on the operator's calendar directly rather than through the champion, using a framing that costs them nothing: 'I want to understand how the work actually gets done so we don't build the wrong thing - 45 minutes, no prep, no slides.' Open every session with the same 60-second block: who you are, why you are there, that there are no wrong answers, that you will record for accuracy and share the write-up back, and an explicit yes/no on recording that you capture in the transcript. Then run a fixed shape - 5 minutes context, 25 minutes past-behaviour and screen-share walkthrough, 10 minutes constraints and metrics, 5 minutes commitments - and hold to it, because a session that runs long is a session the operator will not grant you twice.

resource.label: GOV.UK Service Manual - Getting informed consent for user research

subtopics.name: Laddering: from raw request to decision to business metric
subtopics.learn: Treat every stated request as the top of a ladder and climb down it in the room: 'we need a dashboard' -> what decision does the dashboard support -> who makes that decision, how often, on what data today -> what happens when they get it wrong -> what does that cost per occurrence. Use one-word probes to keep them talking ('and then?', 'because?', 'walk me through that'), and stop laddering at the first number tied to money, time or risk, because that is the level at which the buyer will fund it. Learn Shape Up's distinction between the raw idea and the shaped problem, and the appetite question - 'is this a two-week thing or a two-month thing for you?' - asked of the customer rather than of yourself, so scope gets bounded by their patience, not by your ambition.

resource.label: Shape Up (Basecamp) - Chapter 3: Set Boundaries (appetite, narrowing the problem)

subtopics.name: Workflow archaeology: watch the work, do not ask about the work
subtopics.learn: Get a screen share and make them process a real case in front of you while you stay silent - 'do it exactly as you would if I weren't here, including the bits you'd normally skip'. Count and record the artefacts nobody mentions in a requirements doc: the shadow spreadsheet, the copy-paste between two systems (the swivel chair), the Slack DM that is actually an approval step, the saved email search that is actually a queue, the person they ping when it is ambiguous. Time the case end to end with a stopwatch, note every hand-off and every point where work waits, and ask 'how often is this the easy version?' - the exception path is usually 30 to 60 percent of volume and is where automation dies.

resource.label: NN/g - Contextual Inquiry: observing and interviewing users in their context

subtopics.name: Quantify the pain from their own data, not from their adjectives
subtopics.learn: Convert anecdote to arithmetic before the follow-up call: volume (cases per week), unit cost (minutes per case x loaded hourly rate), error rate, rework rate, and cost of delay (what one day of latency costs). Ask for the smallest real artefact that gets you there - a CSV export of the last 90 days of tickets, a table dump, a query result - and be specific about columns and timeframe so it can be approved as low-risk. Load it in DuckDB (`read_csv_auto`, then `SELECT date_trunc('week', created_at), count(*), median(closed_at - created_at)`), and come back with three numbers, the query that produced them, and one number you are unsure about - inviting the correction is what makes the other two credible.

resource.label: DuckDB docs - CSV Import (read_csv and the CSV sniffer)

subtopics.name: Read the system, not just the people: schemas, APIs and the integration inventory
subtopics.learn: In parallel with the human interviews, ask for the machine-readable truth: an OpenAPI document, a `\d+` schema dump or ERD, five real (redacted) payloads, and a list of every system the process touches. For each system record whether it is the system of record or a system of reference, who owns it internally, whether it has an API or only a CSV export, its auth model, and its rate limits. Then ask the single highest-yield engineering question in discovery - 'what breaks today, and how do you find out?' - because the existing failure modes tell you more about the real architecture than any diagram they will draw for you.

subtopics.name: Constraint discovery: the questions that kill projects if asked late
subtopics.learn: Run a fixed constraint checklist in every engagement before you design anything: where may data physically live and may it leave their VPC or their country; is there egress to third-party model APIs or is this air-gapped; who owns the deploy and what is the change-freeze calendar; what identity provider and what does 'SSO' mean here concretely (Entra, Okta, Keycloak, SAML vs OIDC); what security review, pen test or vendor questionnaire stands between you and production and how long has that taken for the last vendor; what is the data-retention and deletion obligation. Capture each answer with a named owner and a date, and treat 'I think it's fine' as unanswered. Every one of these is cheap in week one and an architecture rewrite in week ten.

subtopics.name: Define the success metric and run the pre-mortem before writing code
subtopics.learn: Write the success metric in SLI form - indicator, measurement method, current baseline, target, date, and who reads it - for example 'median analyst time-to-triage on inbound alerts, measured from webhook receipt to analyst disposition in the DefenderMate audit log, currently 22 minutes, target under 5 minutes for 80 percent of alerts by 31 March, reviewed monthly by the SOC lead'. Insist that the baseline is measured, not remembered, and that the instrumentation to measure it is part of phase one rather than an afterthought. Then run a 15-minute pre-mortem with the champion: 'it is six months from now and this was quietly switched off - write down the three most likely reasons' - and turn each reason into either a discovery question you have not asked or a risk with an owner.

subtopics.name: Opportunity mapping: keeping the problem space separate from the solution space
subtopics.learn: Structure what you heard as an opportunity solution tree: one desired outcome at the root (the metric above), opportunities beneath it phrased as the customer's own unmet needs and pain points in their words, and solutions only as leaves attached to a specific opportunity. Enforce the discipline that a solution with no parent opportunity gets deleted, and that an opportunity supported by one loud stakeholder and zero operators is marked as such. Choose the target opportunity explicitly on reach (how many people, how often), impact on the root metric, your confidence given the evidence count, and effort under the customer's constraints - and write the reason down, because in month three someone will ask why you did not build the other thing.

resource.label: Product Talk (Teresa Torres) - Opportunity Solution Trees

subtopics.name: Interviewing the incumbent engineering team without becoming the threat
subtopics.learn: The customer's own platform or data team is simultaneously your best source of ground truth and the group most likely to quietly stall you, because a vendor arriving with a mandate reads as a verdict on their backlog. Interview them first, not last, and lead with the questions that concede status: 'what have you already tried here', 'what did you build that we should reuse rather than replace', 'what would you have done with another two engineers'. Ask directly what they want to own after go-live and what they refuse to be paged for, then make that split explicit in the problem statement - an FDE who hands over a runbook and an on-call boundary gets change windows; one who does not, does not.

resource.label: Atlassian Team Playbook - Roles and Responsibilities play

subtopics.name: Synthesis: from raw transcript to evidence with a count behind it
subtopics.learn: Within 24 hours of each session, cut the transcript into atomic observations, tag each with speaker, role, and type (fact, quote, pain, workaround, constraint, request, metric), and keep verbatim wording for anything you will later quote back. Cluster across interviews and attach a support count to every claim - 'four of five operators maintain a private spreadsheet' is an insight; 'users want better search' is a paraphrase of one person. Deliberately record disconfirming evidence and the claims that only the champion made, and mark every open question with the person who can close it, so synthesis produces a to-do list rather than a mood.

resource.label: GOV.UK Service Manual - Analyse a research session

subtopics.name: The one-page problem statement the client will actually sign
subtopics.learn: Write one page, in their vocabulary, with six fixed sections: current state with numbers and the query behind them; who is affected and how often; what it costs today; the constraint set with named owners; the success metric with baseline, target and date; and explicit non-goals ('this does not replace the case management system', 'this does not touch PHI in phase one'), plus open questions with owners. Lead with the customer's own quoted words rather than your framing, keep every number traceable to a source, and cut every adjective that is not attached to a measurement. Then do the read-back: send it, get on a call, read it aloud, and ask 'what did I get wrong?' - written agreement without a spoken correction usually means they skimmed it.

subtopics.name: Closing for commitment: advancement versus a polite stall
subtopics.learn: End every session by asking for something that costs the other person real resource - an introduction to the operator or the gatekeeper by name, a data export, read access to a system, a named owner for an open question, or a specific 30-minute slot on a specific day. Learn to distinguish advancement (they did a thing) from a stall dressed as enthusiasm ('this is great, send me something and I'll take it to the team'), and record which you got in the write-up. Treat repeated compliments plus zero commitments as the strongest possible negative signal, and say so in the write-up rather than filing it as validation.

resource.label: The Mom Test - teaching notes on commitment and advancement (chapter 5)

subtopics.name: Build the reusable script and self-scorecard, then run the five
subtopics.learn: Produce a single artefact you will use on real engagements: a 45-minute agenda, the consent line, a 12-question core bank with follow-up probes for each, role-specific branches for buyer / operator / gatekeeper / incumbent engineer, the constraint checklist, the closing-ask menu, and a one-page write-up template. Pair it with a scorecard you fill in after every session - your talk ratio (target under 30 percent), leading questions per hour, number of specific past events obtained, number of numbers obtained, commitments obtained, and one thing you would ask differently. Run all five interviews, score each, and revise the script between sessions so the diffs to the script are themselves the evidence of learning.

resource.label: NN/g - Writing an Effective Guide for a UX Interview

outcomes: You can run a 45-minute discovery session end to end from your own script - consent, context, past-behaviour walkthrough, screen-share observation, constraints, closing ask - and finish on time with the transcript, the scorecard and the write-up committed the same day.
You can show a talk-ratio under 30 percent and a leading-question count that falls measurably from interview one to interview five, evidenced by the tagged transcripts, not by your recollection.

You can take any stated request ('we need a dashboard', 'we need an agent') and ladder it in under ten minutes to the decision it supports, the person who makes that decision, and one number in money, time or risk.
You can turn a customer's raw data export into three defensible baseline numbers with the DuckDB queries attached, and present them with an explicit statement of which one you are least sure about.

You can produce a one-page problem statement that the interviewee confirms verbally with no substantive correction, containing a measured baseline, a dated success metric, named constraint owners and explicit non-goals.

You can name, for any engagement, every stakeholder in the five-role map plus the person who has not yet been in a room with you, and state what each one would have to see to consider the project a success.

You can distinguish, in writing, an advancement from a stall for each of your five sessions, and can point to the specific commitment obtained (intro, export, access, calendar slot) or record its absence as a negative signal.

You can run the constraint checklist cold - data residency, egress, identity provider, change windows, security review, retention - and get every item to either an answer with an owner and date or an explicit 'unknown, blocking'.
failureModes: You interview the champion and the VP, never the analyst who does the work, and ship a workflow whose second step the operations team is contractually forbidden from performing, which nobody discovers until UAT.

You demo Kaupex in the discovery call, get 'wow, that's exactly what we need', log it as validation, and only realise months later that no data export, no system access and no second meeting ever came out of that session.

The stated problem is a solution: they ask for a chatbot over their documentation, you build retrieval, and the real defect is that the documentation is three years stale - so the bot now answers confidently and wrongly at scale, which is worse than the search box it replaced.

Nobody measured the baseline, so at the quarterly review the customer's own analyst produces a number from a different definition that says the system made things slower, and you have no instrumented counter-argument.
Data residency comes up in month three: the customer's legal team will not permit egress to a hosted model API, the entire architecture assumed one, and the replan costs more than the original build.

The customer's platform team was treated as a delivery obstacle rather than interviewed, so they own the deploy, never schedule your change window, and the pilot sits in staging until the sponsor loses interest.
You say 'yes, we can do that' three times in a discovery room, the notes become the SOW, and you spend the engagement delivering scope that was never tied to the success metric or to anyone's budget.
interviewQuestions: A customer signed for 'an AI agent that triages our security alerts'. You get one 45-minute session with the SOC analyst before design starts. Give me your actual first six questions, in order, and tell me what each one is trying to disconfirm.

Your champion tells you the team spends 'hours a day' on manual reconciliation. Walk me through how you convert that into a number you would be willing to put in a board deck, including exactly what artefact you ask for and what you do with it.

How do you tell the difference between a customer who is genuinely enthusiastic and one who is being polite? Give me the concrete signals you look for in the session and the thing you ask for at the end that settles it.

You have finished discovery and concluded that the deliverable named in the signed SOW will not move the metric the buyer cares about. Your champion picked that deliverable and told their VP it would work. What do you do, in what order, and what exactly do you say to the champion?

Design the constraint interview for a healthcare customer who wants patient-intake summarisation. What do you ask, whom do you ask, and which single answer, if it comes back wrong, invalidates your default architecture?

In discovery you find that the customer's own platform team already built half of what you were hired to build, and it mostly works. How does that change your problem statement, your architecture and your relationship with that team?
Give me a time you built the wrong thing because discovery was thin. What was the specific question you failed to ask, how would you have asked it, and what is now in your script because of it?
proofOfWork: A public `discovery-kit` repository that a hiring manager can evaluate in fifteen minutes and another engineer can pick up and use on a live engagement. It contains: (1) the versioned discovery script with its git history visible, so the diffs between interview one and interview five are themselves the evidence of learning, plus the consent line, the role-specific question branches, the constraint checklist and the closing-ask menu; (2) five write-ups against a fixed template, each with its filled-in scorecard (talk ratio, leading questions per hour, specific past events obtained, numbers obtained, commitment obtained or explicitly absent) and a summary chart showing those metrics trending across the five; (3) one fully annotated transcript with every question tagged open / closed / leading / loaded / hypothetical and a short written self-critique of the three worst moments; (4) a `baseline/` folder containing one real (anonymised) data export, the DuckDB queries that turn it into three baseline numbers, and a note on which number is weakest and why; (5) a one-page problem statement for the strongest of the five engagements, written in the interviewee's own quoted language, that they confirmed on a read-back call, with the confirmation email or note included; and (6) a `delta.md` comparing the hypothesis you wrote down before interview one with the final problem statement, naming precisely what you were wrong about and which question surfaced it - the last file being the one that actually demonstrates the skill.
